name: Australia
nickname: Australian National Flag, the Blue Ensign
designer: Ivor Evans, Leslie Hawkins, Egbert Nuttall, Annie Dorrington and William Stevens (joint winners of the 1901 competition)
summary: A blue ensign with the Union Flag in the canton, a large seven-pointed Commonwealth Star beneath it, and the Southern Cross in the fly. It was chosen in a 1901 public competition and became the national flag by law in 1953.
origin: After federation on 1 January 1901, the government held a competition for a federal flag that attracted over 32,000 entries. Five entrants with nearly identical designs shared the prize, and the winning flag was first flown in Melbourne on 3 September 1901, now Australian National Flag Day.
The original Commonwealth Star had six points, for the six states. A seventh point was added in 1908 for the territories, and the stars of the Southern Cross were standardised in 1903.
For decades the Union Flag took precedence and the blue ensign was used mainly by government. The Flags Act 1953 made the blue ensign the Australian National Flag; it received royal assent in 1954.

facts: New Zealand's flag is very similar but has four red, white-edged stars and no Commonwealth Star.
Australia also has two official flags representing Indigenous Australians: the Aboriginal flag and the Torres Strait Islander flag, both proclaimed Flags of Australia in 1995.
The Union Flag in the canton keeps the flag at the centre of periodic debates about a new design and a republic.
clues: A blue ensign with a large seven-pointed star below the canton and a constellation of white stars in the fly.
Its large star once had six points, before territories were added.
Five people with almost identical entries shared first prize in its design competition.
Its neighbour across the sea has a similar flag with red stars.
